clusters.title: Psychosomatic illness diagnoses must be handled with great care | Letters
clusters.neutral_headline: Psychosomatic illness diagnoses must be handled with great care | Letters

items.title: Psychosomatic illness diagnoses must be handled with great care | Letters
items.standfirst: Willemina Rietsema, a GP, says no explanation doesn’t mean no physical illness, it just means we haven’t found one (yet). Carrie Eckersley thinks we need to consider the wider context in which symptoms developRegarding Huw Green’s article (How can we explain psychosomatic illnesses?, 22 November), the body and the mind/brain have strong connections both ways. It is therefore not surprising that major psychological distress can lead to physical symptoms, and the other way around.However, as a GP, I would recommend being extremely careful about equating “otherwise unexplained symptoms” with psychosomatic illness. No explanation doesn’t mean no physical illness, it just means we haven’t found one (yet). Continue reading...

items.title: ‘I felt a zap race through my body’: what happens when someone is hit by lightning?
items.standfirst: Tens of thousands of people experience strikes each year. What are the effects of a current five times hotter than the sun – and how can you keep safe?Caitlin Thomas recalls knowing that something terrible had happened but not fully understanding what.She and her partner had arrived at a music festival some 270km north of Melbourne in the early afternoon and began setting up their tents and a gazebo for shade when the sky suddenly turned dark and the rain became incredibly heavy. A huge gust of wind picked up and Thomas asked her partner to hold on to the gazebo so it wouldn’t fly away. “He then asked me to hold on to it also so he could crack open his beer.” Continue reading...
